Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP Climate science Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August Damien Gayle Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse , which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning. How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more “Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London , which carried out the study. “When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.” View image in fullscreen A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August. It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph. The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off. “Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.” The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event. Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution. Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse. View image in fullscreen ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP Among the study’s key findings were: skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically; July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse; The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost; The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater; A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed. Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology. Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.” View image in fullscreen A major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse. Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The Guardian Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster. Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”. He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.” Explore more on these topics Climate science Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Climate crisis Flooding Nepal Tibet Extreme weather news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods ‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silence ‘They’ll be finding bodies next year’: a renowned forensic scientist on Nepal’s ‘extreme challenges’ Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster China is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaigners Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels ‘The house got carried 100 metres away’: some Nepal flood victims had minutes of notice. https://astanatimes.com/2026/09/kazakhst.text: Thursday, 8 October, 2026 Almaty 66 °F / 19 °C Astana 52 °F / 11 °C All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Expands Bilateral Ties at UN General Assembly By Dana Omirgazy in Editor’s Picks , International on 24 September 2026 ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched an active diplomatic agenda at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, with Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi holding talks with counterparts from several countries and discussing global peace, security and humanitarian law on Sept. 23 in New York. Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi. Photo credit: Kazakh Foreign Ministry Expanding bilateral partnerships On the first day of the General Assembly’s High-Level Week in New York, Tileuberdi held talks with his counterparts from Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Slovenia, Ukraine and El Salvador, the ministry’s press service reported. The discussions focused on bilateral cooperation, prospects for expanding political dialogue and trade and economic ties, as well as key international and regional topics. Tileuberdi also met with UN Under-Secretary-General and UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Executive Director Rebecca Grynspan, a candidate for UN Secretary-General, and UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany. The meetings addressed ways to strengthen cooperation with UN institutions and improve the effectiveness of multilateral mechanisms. Focus on peace and security Tileuberdi also took part in a high-level discussion, Reaffirming the Promise of Peace: Using the Power We Have, which focused on conflict prevention and resolution, preventive diplomacy, mediation and strengthening partnerships within the international system. Participants exchanged views on strengthening the UN’s role in maintaining international peace and security and using existing mechanisms more effectively to settle disputes peacefully. New diplomatic relations An important outcome of the first day was the establishment of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and the Central African Republic. The two countries’ foreign ministers signed a joint communiqué confirming their interest in developing bilateral ties and cooperation on international platforms. Tileuberdi also participated in a working meeting of foreign ministers of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) member states, where participants discussed priorities for cooperation between the CSTO and the UN. Kazakhstan promotes compliance with Humanitarian Law At a separate meeting with foreign ministers of the founding states of the Global Initiative to Strengthen Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) President Mirjana Spoljaric, Tileuberdi stressed that the effectiveness of international humanitarian law should be measured by its ability to protect civilians and medical and humanitarian personnel, safeguard critical civilian infrastructure and ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance. The meeting brought together the founding states – Kazakhstan, Brazil, China, France, Jordan and South Africa – to discuss preparations for the Humanity in War high-level conference, scheduled for Dec. 7 in Jordan. Tileuberdi emphasized that international humanitarian law must be applied universally, consistently and in good faith, without selectivity or politicization. Following the meeting, the founding states and the ICRC called on the international community to join the Initiative, strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and ensure high-level participation at the upcoming conference in Jordan. https://www.seznamzpravy.cz/clanek/zahra.text: Chcete-li článek poslouchat, přihlaste se Policisté zaujali pozice po střelbě ve Washingtonu, 12. listopadu 2026 Jeden člověk zemřel a další čtyři utrpěli zranění při střelbě v prestižní washingtonské čtvrti Logan Circle nedaleko Bílého domu. Podezřelý se po činu zabarikádoval v bytě a podle zdrojů stanice NBC News spáchal sebevraždu. Čtyři zraněné a jednoho mrtvého si ve čtvrtek vyžádala střelba v prestižní washingtonské čtvrti v pěší vzdálenosti od Bílého domu, píše agentura AP s odkazem na policii. Podle svědka AP byl jeden člověk z pětice postřelen v posilovně a zraněním podlehl. Podezřelý se podle policie po příjezdu strážníků zabarikádoval a následně se střelil. Podle dvou bezpečnostních zdrojů stanice NBC News je podezřelý po smrti. Střelba byla hlášena ve čtvrti Logan Circle zhruba 1,6 kilometru od Bílého domu. Prozatímní šéf metropolitní policie Jeffrey Carroll uvedl, že jedna z obětí zemřela. Podezřelý, který měl zřejmě spor se společenstvím vlastníků, se podle Carrolla po střelbě zabarikádoval v bytě a po telefonátu s policií se střelil a přestal komunikovat. Policie poté do bytu vnikla a našla muže se střelnými poraněními, které si způsobil sám. Podle policie byt zřejmě patřil podezřelému. Stanice NBC News s odkazem na dva bezpečnostní zdroje píše, že střelec je po smrti. Policie vyzvala veřejnost, aby se vyhnula oblasti, kde se nachází fitness centrum VIDA, episkopální kostel sv. Lukáše a obytné domy. Velká část bloku kolem 15. ulice byla uzavřena páskou a ve školách v oblasti byla vyhlášena uzávěra. Při policejním zásahu byly uzavřeny i přilehlé ulice. Federální Úřad pro alkohol, tabák, zbraně a výbušniny (ATF) uvedl, že na místo vyslal své agenty, aby se zásahem pomohli. Policejnímu vyšetřování pomáhá místní pobočka Federálního úřadu pro vyšetřování (FBI). Podezřelý podle úřadů zastřelil nejméně jednoho člověka v posilovně, načež vyšel ven a pokračoval ve střelbě, postřelil mimo jiné jednoho člověka ve výtahu k parkovišti. Poté se zabarikádoval v bytě v sedmém patře domu. Na střechu a ke vchodu byly vyslány zásahové jednotky. Svědek agentury AP James Spellman, který byl v době střelby v posilovně, uvedl, že jeden člověk byl střelen do krku, skácel se k zemi a zemřel na místě. V posilovně tehdy podle svědka bylo asi 50 osob a byly slyšet dva výstřely uvnitř a asi šest venku. Všichni prchali ven. Nejde o první násilnosti v této čtvrti. Podle úřadů byl začátkem srpna 2025 v časných nedělních hodinách ve čtvrti Logan Circle napaden bývalý člen útvaru pro efektivitu státní správy (DOGE) prezidenta Donalda Trumpa skupinou mladistvých, kteří se jemu a jedné ženě pokusili ukrást auto. O několik dní později Trump obešel místní samosprávu, zavedl nad městem přímou federální kontrolu a vyslal do něj stovky příslušníků Národní gardy s cílem snížit kriminalitu.
